item.text: Soruları altı parçadan sırayla alıp tek JSONL dosyasında Türkçeleştireceğim; ardından belirtilen denetimi çalıştıracağım.

{"id": "23:1/q13", "question": "How is the Garden's speech and God's hand understood?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q13/p1", "position": "The Garden's speech signifies that it has been prepared for believers, and God's hand signifies His direct creation.", "reasons": "Razi compares the personified response of heaven and earth at 41:11 and says God undertook Eden's creation personally. He treats prayer's praising and interceding for a good worshipper, or condemning a neglectful one, as figurative because movements cannot literally speak; he compares saying a benefactor's kindness speaks gratitude."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q14", "question": "What happened when the opening ten verses were revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q14/p1", "position": "The Prophet heard revelation like buzzing bees, prayed for divine favor, then said whoever upholds the ten verses enters Paradise.", "reasons": "Umar's reports vary in prayer wording: increase, honor, giving, divine approval and contentment; Ahmad, Ali ibn al-Madini and others add contentment. He faced the qibla and raised his hands in some versions. Al-Nahhas glosses upholding as observing without violating the teachings; Qurtubi adds later ablution and pilgrimage obligations. Ibn al-Arabi authenticated the report, while al-Tirmidhi called it munkar because only unknown Yunus ibn Sulaym transmits it; al-Nasai and al-Hakim also transmitted it. Kur'an Yolu cites it for the afterlife sense."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q15", "question": "How did Aisha describe the Prophet's character through this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q15/p1", "position": "She recited the opening through those guarding prayer and said these traits were his character.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and Suyuti report her broader statement that his character was the Quran."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q16", "question": "What is reported about the Prophet reciting this sūra in prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q16/p1", "position": "At Mecca's conquest he began the sūra while praying at the Kaaba, coughed near the mention of Moses and Jesus or Aaron, then bowed.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites al-Nasai and Muslim from Abd Allah ibn al-Saib; Ibn Ashur gives al-Nasai's version and Abu Dawud's dawn-prayer variant, where he cut the recitation short."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q17", "question": "What other reports connect this passage to revelation or recitation?", "turns_on": "These are distinct transmitted claims about the passage.", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q17/p1", "position": "Reciting this sūra brings angels' glad tidings of comfort at death.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b from the Prophet."}, {"id": "23:1/q17/p2", "position": "The qualities were revealed also to Abraham, and only Abraham and Muhammad fulfilled them.", "reasons": "Abu Umama connects passages of 9:112, 23:1, 33:35 and 70:23 in the report cited by Suyuti."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q18", "question": "What was the sūra's place and manner of revelation?", "turns_on": "The sources address both location and batching of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q18/p1", "position": "It was revealed in Mecca.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Jishumi's al-Qadi, Abu Hayyan, Baydawi, Suyuti's Ibn Abbas and Study Quran affirm it; Ibn Ashur calls it consensus and rejects an inference of Medinan revelation from zakah. Asad says most classical commentators place it late in Mecca; some call it the final Meccan revelation, which he finds inconclusive."}, {"id": "23:1/q18/p2", "position": "The opening was revealed as one of the Quran's batches of verses according to need.", "reasons": "Suyuti uses the opening alongside the Ifk passage, a single phrase and part of another verse to illustrate revelation in groups of varying length."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q19", "question": "How many verses does the sūra contain?", "turns_on": "The reported regional verse counts differ, especially the Basran count.", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q19/p1", "position": "It has 118 verses by Kufan count and 117 by Basran count.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits this from al-Qadi."}, {"id": "23:1/q19/p2", "position": "It has 118 verses by Kufan count and 119 by Basran count.", "reasons": "Baydawi gives these counts."}, {"id": "23:1/q19/p3", "position": "It has 118 verses.", "reasons": "Suyuti states this without a regional distinction."}, {"id": "23:1/q19/p4", "position": "It has 118 verses by Kufan count and 110 by Basran count.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives these counts."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q20", "question": "Why is the sūra called al-Mu'minun, and what other names has it?", "turns_on": "The title can name the opening believers, quote its wording, or use the success word.", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q20/p1", "position": "Its title comes from the believers and the success announced at its opening.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur gives both an association with its theme and an alternative that the title quotes the exact opening word; Biqai says the title plainly states the sūra's purpose."}, {"id": "23:1/q20/p2", "position": "It is also called Qad Aflaha or Surat al-Falah.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites Ibn al-Qasim's report about Malik's grandfather's Uthman-era mushaf notation, contrasted with a reading at 23:85."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q21", "question": "What is the sūra's overall argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q21/p1", "position": "It assigns success to believers, describes their virtues, and warns the denying or powerful opponents.", "reasons": "Biqai makes believers' special success the purpose; Tabatabai describes a Meccan call to God and the Last Day, believers' service, unbelievers' vices and warnings through the histories from Noah to Jesus. Study Quran observes repeated opposition by the affluent and powerful, comparing 7:59–62 and 7:136. Asad makes belief in a conscious Creator imply afterlife belief; Islahi sees the promised Paradise subject to conditions."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q22", "question": "How does the opening connect to the end of al-Hajj?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q22/p1", "position": "It announces the success hoped for after al-Hajj's commands to worship and do good.", "reasons": "Jishumi sees the opening detailing al-Hajj's final commands. Abu Hayyan cites 22:77. Biqai lists prayer, zakah and divine protection as duties yielding good in both lives. Islahi calls the sūras counterparts on the community's duty to witness true religion, with different styles and temporary trials. Samarrai matches the commands at 22:77–78 to the traits at 23:1–4, and says qad confirms their quick fulfillment."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q23", "question": "How does the sūra's ending answer its opening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q23/p1", "position": "Its closing denial of unbelievers' success contrasts with the opening affirmation for believers.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, al-Kirmani, Islahi and Samarrai cite the close at 23:117; Islahi notes that detailed believer traits and unbeliever humiliation give the two ends force."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q24", "question": "What other passages or sūras connect with this opening?", "turns_on": "The notes point to different cross-sūra relationships.", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q24/p1", "position": "The next sūra, al-Nur, develops faith's light in individual and collective life.", "reasons": "Islahi says al-Nur supplements this sūra by showing faith's inward illumination and the darkness of its absence."}, {"id": "23:1/q24/p2", "position": "Al-Mu'minun describes faith generally, while al-Ma'arij specifies belief in Judgment.", "reasons": "Samarrai says this sūra's account is thus more comprehensive."}, {"id": "23:1/q24/p3", "position": "The believers' reward can be described as inheritance or exchange.", "reasons": "Qurtubi refers to an exchange discussed at 64:9 and to inheritance under al-Mu'minun's opening."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q25", "question": "What related notes are given on the basmala and the divine name at this opening?", "turns_on": "The sources comment on different aspects of the opening formula.", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q25/p1", "position": "The name conveys primordial loftiness and knowing Bismillah raises aspiration and brings unexpected heart knowledge.", "reasons": "Qushayri derives the name from elevation and links it to the Real's primordial loftiness."}, {"id": "23:1/q25/p2", "position": "The basmala presents sovereign mercy given generally through explanation and particularly through faith.", "reasons": "Biqai distinguishes al-Rahman as comprehensive mercy and al-Rahim as singling out those chosen for faith."}]}
{"id": "23:1/q26", "question": "Where does the opening passage allow a necessary stop in recitation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:1/q26/p1", "position": "Its story endings are among places where necessity licenses stopping.", "reasons": "Suyuti transmits Ibn al-Jazari's preferred examples, including paired directions, prophets, prayer and almsgiving, and story endings in this sūra."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q01", "question": "How does this relative clause describe the believers?", "turns_on": "Whether the listed attributes delimit believers or describe the fruit and grounds of faith.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q01/p1", "position": "It is an adjectival relative clause qualifying the believers.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās makes الذين nominative as an adjective of المؤمنون and analyzes هم as subject and خاشعون as predicate within the relative clause; following clauses are parallel."}, {"id": "23:2/q01/p2", "position": "The repeated relative clauses present rooted traits as grounds for success.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says each trait evidences rooted faith and is a cause of success, without exhausting all piety; he compares the condemned who failed in prayer, feeding the poor and belief in Judgment (74:42–46). Jishumī says the traits clarify who is a believer; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says living faith produces effects and success."}, {"id": "23:2/q01/p3", "position": "The traits

restrict true believers, or clarify and praise them.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports both analyses: restriction if the attributes distinguish true believers, or clarification and praise if they are branches of faith; he says some reports support restriction."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q02", "question": "How is ṣalāt read here?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣalāt is taken as a verbal noun or a name for distinct prayers.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q02/p1", "position": "Most readers use the singular form.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports the non-Kufan reading and ʿĀṣim's as singular. Abū ʿAlī treats it as a verbal noun."}, {"id": "23:2/q02/p2", "position": "Kufan readers except ʿĀṣim use the plural form.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports this reading. Abū ʿAlī explains the plural as naming distinct kinds of prescribed prayer, strengthened by its technical legal sense and additions to the original language."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q03", "question": "Why is prayer singular here and plural at the passage's end?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q03/p1", "position": "The singular denotes prayer as a genus; the plural denotes the several prayers to be guarded.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, as reported by Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn, specifies five prayers, witr and regular sunnas or other optional services. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says humility applies uniformly to prayer as a kind, while maintenance concerns each obligatory prayer."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q04", "question": "Why is prayer called 'their prayer'?", "turns_on": "Whether the possessive stresses benefit or the believers' close connection with prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q04/p1", "position": "The worshippers own its benefit, while God needs nothing from it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī calls prayer their provision and treasure; al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī repeat the benefit contrast. Al-Biqāʿī says the ascription encourages guarding prayer as the bond between them and God."}, {"id": "23:2/q04/p2", "position": "The possessive conveys close attachment to prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts this close relation with merely saying they are humble whenever they pray."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q05", "question": "Why is 'in their prayer' placed before 'humble'?", "turns_on": "Which force of the fronted phrase is intended: emphasis, connection, or restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q05/p1", "position": "It emphasizes prayer and suits the verse-end pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn cites emphasis and the end-rhyme shared with parallel verses. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the order gives care and priority to prayer as Islam's most important pillar."}, {"id": "23:2/q05/p2", "position": "It connects prayer tightly to the believers and their faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the wording attaches humility closely to their own prayer. Ālūsī reports that prayer is brought near faith because prayer is itself called faith at 2:143."}, {"id": "23:2/q05/p3", "position": "It restricts the claim to all of their prayers.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this as another explanation, against humility in only some prayers."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q06", "question": "What does 'humble' convey as an enduring description?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q06/p1", "position": "The nominal wording makes humility a lasting trait through prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts a verbal expression and notes its concise force; al-Sāmarrāʾī says it should persist in heart and limbs throughout prayer. He also reads 22:77–78's commands as stable believer qualities here."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q07", "question": "What does khushūʿ mean in this prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names its inward cause, outward sign, both together, or a particular act.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q07/p1", "position": "Humble submission and reverence before God.", "reasons": "Muqātil describes submission so complete one misses neighbors; Ṭabarī includes obedient performance of prescribed prayer, still limbs and avoiding forbidden things and refuses restriction to one sign. Zajjāj cites subdued voices at 20:108 for the root. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, Ibn ʿĪsā and later exegetes gloss humility and abasement. Islāhī adduces 20:108 and 57:16 for inward submission expressed in posture, recitation and prostration; Kur'an Yolu cites Ṭabarī's obedience and respect."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p2", "position": "Fear and awe within the heart.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda recur in early transmissions; Ibn ʿAbbās combines fear with stillness. Al-Wāḥidī says fear explains why one is still rather than defining the root. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes fear producing reverence, with 2:45 and 21:90. Al-Kāshshāf and Bayḍāwī add the lowered gaze; Bursawī adds humility and gaze fixed on prayer. The Qurʾān Yolu translation is deep reverence."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p3", "position": "Stillness, quiet and dignified bodily composure.", "reasons": "Al-Zuhrī, Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm and ʿAmr ibn Dīnār repeatedly supply this gloss; the latter denies that bowing and prostrating alone suffice. Al-Wāḥidī makes stillness the Arabic root sense and reduces lowering the eyes and person to it. Ibn al-Jawzī cites 41:39. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says bodily lowering shows a fearful heart. Al-Sāmarrāʾī adds abstention from unnecessary movement and distractions."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p4", "position": "Lowered gaze, head and demeanor.", "reasons": "Mujāhid adds gentleness, lowered voice or wing; Ibn Masʿūd lowered gaze, hands and voice. Al-Mawārdī notes keeping the gaze within the prayer place. Muslim ibn Yasār and Qatāda specify the prostration place or bowed head. Majāz adds remaining bowed; Study Quran cites root images of lowliness and withering at 54:7, 68:43, 70:44, 79:9."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p5", "position": "Not turning during prayer, with gentleness toward others.", "reasons": "ʿAlī includes not turning and softness toward a Muslim; al-Rabīʿ, ʿAlī and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr stress staying absorbed enough not to notice either side. Ibn ʿAbbās likewise says fear makes neighbors unnoticed."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p6", "position": "A condition of the heart alone.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda are cited for the heart alone; Qatāda, ʿAlī and Ibrāhīm also locate it there. The bodily signs follow the heart as ruler. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a heart state that can exist outside prayer; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls attribution to limbs figurative and cites humbled voices at 20:108. Al-Mufradāt instead says khushūʿ usually shows in limbs and khudūʿ is more often inward."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p7", "position": "An act of bodily limbs alone.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this as an alternative; al-Rāzī and Elmalılı report bodily stillness and not turning as an independent definition. Al-Rāzī says only the bodily signs are visible."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p8", "position": "Heart and limbs together, with inner fear appearing outwardly.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports heart and sight; al-Jishumī prefers outward submission with inward reverence. Al-Baghawī distinguishes khushūʿ in heart, body, sight and voice from merely bodily khudūʿ, while al-Layth locates it in sight and voice and calls soft ground khashʿa. Al-Rāzī and Elmalılı prefer inward surrender expressed by still lowered eyes; al-Ṭabrisī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī say the heart governs limbs. Al-Nasafī, Biqāʿī, Ālūsī, Islāhī and al-Sāmarrāʾī likewise combine them."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p9", "position": "Exclusive inward attention to prayer and God.", "reasons": "Some define it as gathering one's full attention and turning away from everything else. Ibn Kathīr and al-Biqāʿī say emptying the heart and preferring prayer makes it rest and delight. Ṭabāṭabāʾī pictures a subdued person entirely occupied with an overpowering presence. Al-Qāshānī describes awe at the light of majesty. Ibn ʿĀshūr says prayer especially stirs the heart because it is intimate address."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p10", "position": "Placing the right hand over the left.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives this concrete interpretation in al-Thaʿlabī; al-Ḍaḥḥāk is cited for it by Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p11", "position": "Repentance.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes the gloss to Ibrāhīm."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p12", "position": "Reverence, sincere speech, certainty and focused aspiration.", "reasons": "The saying continued by al-Thaʿlabī gives these four conditions; Abū al-Dardāʾ is named in al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī. The position concerns reverence for the standing place and full collected attention."}, {"id": "23:2/q07/p13", "position": "Sincere prayer for God without seeking a return.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports Abū Bakr al-Wāsiṭī's gloss."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q08", "question": "What happened to worshippers' gaze when this verse was revealed?", "turns_on": "The reports vary over the subject, earlier direction of gaze and certainty of the occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q08/p1", "position": "The Prophet had looked skyward, then lowered his gaze to his prayer or prostration place.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīrīn and Abū Hurayra transmit the widely repeated account. Versions say he lowered his head or looked at the ground; al-Ḥākim authenticated Abū Hurayra's report. Ibn Kathīr calls Ibn Sīrīn and ʿAṭāʾ's reports mursal; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and al-Kāshshāf state no grading."}, {"id": "23:2/q08/p2", "position": "The Prophet had looked around or right and left, then bowed his head and looked down.", "reasons": "A narrator other than ʿAṭāʾ and versions from Ibn Sīrīn mention looking around; one says he looked at something while praying and raised his gaze. Some accounts combine turning and upward gaze."}, {"id": "23:2/q08/p3", "position": "The Companions had looked upward, then lowered heads or gazes.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīrīn, Abū Hurayra and others transmit this; one version says they had also turned and then ceased looking around. Suyūṭī calls Ibn Sīrīn's report mursal."}, {"id": "23:2/q08/p4", "position": "Muslims had looked sideways, then faced forward toward the qibla.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya's report specifies looking forward, or toward
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

 the Kaʿba in the sanctuary. Hushaym's version says the Muslims faced their prayer. Al-Thaʿlabī combines skyward and sideways looking."}, {"id": "23:2/q08/p5", "position": "The connection of the Prophet's lowered gaze to this very verse was uncertain.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīrīn reports an unnamed informant who did not know whether this verse was the occasion; the practice of keeping the gaze on the prayer place remains in the report."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q09", "question": "Where should the gaze be directed during prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the norm is the prostration place or forward qibla and what counts as an invalidating turn.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q09/p1", "position": "Toward the place of prostration, within the prayer place.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīrīn and others give this practice; Ibn Kathīr transmits advice to close one's eyes if accustomed to looking around. Al-Kāshshāf, al-Bayḍāwī and others link it to reverent fear; Ibn ʿUmar adds awareness that God attends to the worshipper. Al-Nutaf dislikes looking skyward at the opening takbīr as a prohibited turning, though skyward looking outside prayer is acceptable for supplication. Ālūsī prohibits raising the eyes even for a blind person, citing Jābir ibn Samura's warning in Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah that sight may not return."}, {"id": "23:2/q09/p2", "position": "Face forward toward the qibla; in Mecca look at the Sacred House.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives the direction as qibla or ahead and specifies Kaʿba in the sanctuary. Kashifī distinguishes standing outside Mecca, with gaze at the prostration place, from Mecca, with gaze at the House. Study Quran notes that some worshippers look forward and slightly down."}, {"id": "23:2/q09/p3", "position": "A side glance without turning the neck need not invalidate prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Nasāʾī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet glanced right and left without twisting his neck; Kaʿb says the Prophet saw his glance but did not require repetition. Al-Qurṭubī points to his discussion of the direction faced at 2:144."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q10", "question": "Which movements and distractions conflict with humility in prayer?", "turns_on": "How far particular bodily acts, glances and distractions infringe the verse's humility.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q10/p1", "position": "Turning, fidgeting and worldly distraction should be avoided.", "reasons": "Mujāhid says scholars disliked hand fidgeting, looking around and worldly thought. ʿĀʾisha reports turning as Satan's theft, in al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī; Abū Dharr reports God's attention turns away when the worshipper turns. Abū Hurayra reports divine attention calling the person back, and Ālūsī's report allows an unavoidable turn only outside the obligatory part. ʿAṭāʾ prohibits fiddling with any limb; Abū Dharr's report says not to move pebbles because mercy faces the worshipper, cited by al-Tirmidhī; al-Ḥasan rebukes a pebble fidgeter seeking a heavenly bride."}, {"id": "23:2/q10/p2", "position": "Prayer manners encompass restrained clothing, posture, mouth, eyes and hands.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū Ḥayyān list avoiding bunched clothing, bodily or clothing fidgeting, turning, stretching, yawning, closing eyes, covering mouth, trailing clothing, cracking or interlacing fingers, hands on hips and shifting pebbles; Ālūsī repeats much of this. Ālūsī calls hand-on-hip posture disliked, explaining the 'rest of the people of Hell' as a Jewish practice rather than actual rest in Hell (43:75)."}, {"id": "23:2/q10/p3", "position": "Swaying should cease so limbs remain still.", "reasons": "Ālūsī calls swaying prohibited as a Jewish practice. Umm Rūmān reports Abū Bakr citing the Prophet's instruction not to sway like Jews and that still limbs complete prayer; Elmalılı repeats it."}, {"id": "23:2/q10/p4", "position": "Outward restraint is prescribed as the fruit of a humble heart.", "reasons": "The Prophet's response to the man playing with his beard is repeated widely: if his heart were humble, his limbs would be humble. Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes a version to an unnamed scholar; Ālūsī calls Abū Hurayra's version weak; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes no grading. Bursawī gives the general heart-to-limbs report."}]}
{"id": "23:2/q11", "question": "Is khushūʿ in prayer obligatory?", "turns_on": "Whether the demand governs legal validity, the duty to pray, acceptance, or completeness.", "positions": [{"id": "23:2/q11/p1", "position": "Yes, it is obligatory.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī asserts this; al-Baghawī says the later mention of guarding prayer shows both preservation and humility obligatory. Al-Rāzī grounds the duty in reflection on recitation (47:24, 73:4), remembrance (20:14), the ban on heedlessness (7:205), and the analogy to knowing what one says while intoxicated (4:43). Al-Qurṭubī and al-Taḥrīr judge this the correct view, locating it in the heart."}, {"id": "23:2/q11/p2", "position": "It is a meritorious completion of prayer.", "reasons": "The juristic alternative is reported by al-Qurṭubī and al-Taḥrīr; Ibn Ḥajar's commentary on al-Minhāj recommends inward and outward humility throughout prayer, including attention and avoiding purposeless motion."}, {"id": "23:2/q11/p3", "position": "Prayer without it still discharges the formal obligation, though acceptance and reward may fail.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī answers the objection from juristic consensus by distinguishing legal discharge from acceptance, comparing a returned garment given courteously or contemptuously. Al-Ālūsī rejects making inward humility a validity component, although some jurists require it for some part; he cites sound reports for the loss of reward. Elmalılı links the inward root to valid intention and outward signs to manners. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says a non-praying person has not performed the pillar at all."}, {"id": "23:2/q11/p4", "position": "Heedless prayer is corrupt or earns only its understood portion.", "reasons": "Bishr al-Ḥāfī calls a prayer without khushūʿ corrupt, al-Ḥasan says it approaches punishment, and Muʿādh says deliberate notice of neighbors leaves no prayer. Theologians require inner intention to distinguish prostration to God from an idol. Al-Rāzī prefers the scrupulous view as safer and cites reports granting only a sixth or tenth, or only what is comprehended; ʿAbd al-Wāḥid claims consensus on the last point. Abū al-Layth adds accurate and reflective recitation."}]}

The poetry's attribution is doubted by Ibn ʿĀshūr."}, {"id": "23:4/q06/p5", "position": "The verb faʿala suggests prompt action to meet the poor's needs.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān contrasts ʿamila for sustained good work with faʿala for hastening to do good, citing fa-stabiqū al-khayrāt. Al-Itqān likewise says ʿamila commonly denotes extended work, while faʿala marks quick action."}]}
{"id": "23:4/q07", "question": "What effect do the fronting and repeated relative construction have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:4/q07/p1", "position": "Fronting zakāh marks emphasis, care, or restriction to proper action.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says moving fāʿilūn before zakāh or altering lām changes the layered force; fronting can imply doing only good, including zakāh. Al-Ālūsī allows focus without restriction, or contrast with improper spending; he extends earlier explanations for 'turning away' from idle talk rather than mere nonparticipation. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fronting and repeated relative follow the same construction as earlier traits."}]}
{"id": "23:4/q08", "question": "How does this trait relate to prayer and the neighboring traits?", "turns_on": "The notes connect zakāh to prayer as complementary duties and to the wider list of traits; one comparison distinguishes what completes each duty.", "positions": [{"id": "23:4/q08/p1", "position": "Prayer and zakāh pair bodily worship with financial worship.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say this shows comprehensive devotion; al-Ālūsī says avoiding idle talk lies between them because it connects closely with prayer, although the Qurʾān often pairs the duties. Ibn ʿĀshūr also notes their frequent pairing and an earlier explained thematic reason for the interruption. Iṣlāḥī calls them faith's two arms: prayer joins one to God and zakāh to people; gratitude makes each complement the other."}, {"id": "23:4/q08/p2", "position": "The traits collectively cover duties and identify successful believers.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says duties omitted by name fall under trusts and covenants, while sins fall under avoidance of laghw; the list clearly identifies believers. Iṣlāḥī traces faith through prayer, zakāh, restraint, fidelity and guarded prayer to lasting success, and summarizes the opening similarly. Study Quran describes the opening as believers' virtues and righteous acts. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says living faith works toward success."}, {"id": "23:4/q08/p3", "position": "The prescribed payment completes zakāh, while prayer needs inward humility to complete its outward acts.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes the two obligations: prayer also requires reflection, presence of heart and proper manners. He cites a Prophetic saying that one receives from prayer only what one consciously understands; Iṣlāḥī says earlier discussion of humble, fearful prayer preventing sin leads to further benefits."}]}
{"id": "23:4/q09", "question": "How does the verse connect with other Qurʾānic passages or the wider sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:4/q09/p1", "position": "Al-Ḥajj's commands become the stable believer qualities listed here.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares bowing, prostration, doing good, establishing prayer and giving zakāh in 22:77–78 with 23:1–4; imperative actions become nominal descriptions of humility, avoiding idle talk and giving."}, {"id": "23:4/q09/p2", "position": "This verse's zakāh is broader than al-Maʿārij's specified share for the asker and deprived.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares 70:24–25: this wording reaches financial worship across eight recipient classes and purification of the self as well as the specified share."}, {"id": "23:4/q09/p3", "position": "Al-Nūr supplements al-Muʾminūn's opening account of faithful life.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says faith illuminating the inner self brightens individual and collective life in the next sūra, while lack of faith darkens both."}, {"id": "23:4/q09/p4", "position": "The sura's broader narrative repeatedly shows powerful and affluent opponents of prophets.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites parallels in 7:59–62 and 7:136. Al-Qurṭubī says the meanings of idle talk and zakāh were already treated at al-Baqara, mentioning 2:219."}]}
{"id": "23:4/q10", "question": "What inward meaning is given to zakāh?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:4/q10/p1", "position": "It is detachment from one's own traits and self-witness.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls their zakāh detachment from their own traits. Al-Qushayrī takes zakāh as growth but says spiritual growth needs diminishing one's witness of self; complete servitude follows the dissolution of that witness."}]}
{"id": "23:4/q11", "question": "What is reported about the first ten verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:4/q11/p1", "position": "Whoever upholds them enters Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports ʿUmar describing the bee-like sound of revelation and the Prophet's supplication before relating this promise."}]}
{"id": "23:4/q12", "question": "When does wealth become zakāh?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:4/q12/p1", "position": "Only when it reaches the poor recipient.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this view of when the paid wealth acquires the name zakāh."}]}
{"id": "23:8/q01", "question": "How is the word for trusts read?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun is expressed as one collective or verbal noun or as multiple individual trusts, with ʿahd and 4:58 offered as analogies; sources differ on the named singular readers.", "positions": [{"id": "23:8/q01/p1", "position": "It is read in the plural, amānātihim.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās prefers the plural because God entrusted many duties, including purification, prayer, and fasting, but rejects Abū ʿUbayd's inference from 4:58: that verse concerns particular deposits, and singular ʿahd here permits either number. Ibn Khālawayh, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Abū ʿAlī through al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Samīn cite 4:58 for the plural; al-Wāḥidī compares singular collective 6:108 with plural 23:63. Al-Samīn prefers the plural for its generality. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it explicitly covers numerous kinds and trustees. Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr are included among singular readers in some accounts, despite accounts naming Ibn Kathīr alone; al-Naḥḥās reports Meccans and al-Nasafī Meccans and Sahl. Al-Baghawī's cited command is noted as 4:57. Qirāʾāt-ER says the plural individualizes obligations."}, {"id": "23:8/q01/p2", "position": "It is read in the singular, amānatihim.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr is repeatedly named, here and at 70:32; Ibn Mujāhid and al-Fārisī call him the sole singular reader, while al-Rāzī also names Nāfiʿ, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī mention a transmission from Abū ʿAmr, al-Naḥḥās says Meccans, and al-Nasafī adds Sahl. Ibn Khālawayh, al-Thaʿlabī, Jishumī, and al-Baghawī point to singular ʿahd; al-Wāḥidī and Abū ʿAlī say the singular verbal or collective noun embraces multiple trusts; Ibn al-Jawzī calls it generic. Al-Bayḍāwī says it avoids ambiguity or retains the original verbal noun; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 23:2. Al-Ṭabrisī cites a Prophetic statement on a woman's womb and 2:228 as an example of singular usage. Qirāʾāt-ER says it treats trust as one abstract concept."}]}
